description: Test your knowledge of Histology & Embryology (Neuroanatomy) for MBBS examination.

cards.text: What is the characteristic shape of grey matter in a spinal cord cross-section, and what does each horn contain?
cards.answer: H-shaped or butterfly-shaped grey matter. Anterior horn contains large multipolar alpha motor neurons; posterior horn contains smaller neurons with substantia gelatinosa (pain modulation); lateral horn (T1–L2 only) contains preganglionic sympathetic neurons.

tip.tip: Remember: Anterior = motors (large), Posterior = pain (small), Lateral = sympathetic (T1–L2 only)

cards.text: Describe Purkinje cells: location, appearance, and their role in the cerebellum.
cards.answer: Large, flask-shaped neurons in the middle layer (Purkinje cell layer) of cerebellar cortex. They have extensive dendritic trees in the molecular layer. They are GABAergic (inhibitory) and are the ONLY output of the cerebellar cortex, inhibiting deep cerebellar nuclei.

tip.tip: Purkinje = flask-shaped, inhibitory output; like a 'Purkinje bottleneck' controlling cerebellar output

cards.text: What is unique about granule cells in the cerebellum?
cards.answer: Granule cells are the most numerous neurons in the entire central nervous system. They are located in the granular (deepest) layer of cerebellar cortex, are excitatory (glutamate), and send parallel fibres upward to the molecular layer where they synapse with Purkinje dendrites.

tip.tip: Granule cells = most numerous CNS neuron; remember 'grain-ule' as the densest layer

cards.text: Compare the architecture of motor cortex (area 4) vs. sensory cortex (areas 1,2,3).
cards.answer: Motor cortex: very thick layer V (Betz cells for output), absent or thin layer IV (no thalamic input) = agranular. Sensory cortex: prominent thick layer IV (thalamic input), thin layer V (less output) = koniocortex ('dust cortex').

tip.tip: Motor thick V, no IV. Sensory thick IV, thin V. Think: 'V = out, IV = in'

cards.text: What are the functions of layer IV and layer V in the cerebral cortex?
cards.answer: Layer IV (internal granular): receives thalamic (sensory) input—the main entry point for information into cortex. Layer V (internal pyramidal): contains Betz cells and pyramidal neurons that provide major output to brainstem and spinal cord (corticospinal tract).

tip.tip: IV = IN (input from thalamus), V = VIA Out (major output pathway)

cards.text: What is substantia gelatinosa (Rolando), and what is its function?
cards.answer: Substantia gelatinosa is the tip of the posterior horn of spinal grey matter, appearing as a dark, compact area due to dense small neurons. It processes pain and temperature information and is involved in pain modulation.

tip.tip: Gelatinosa = gel-like, compact tip of posterior horn; related to pain, not movement

cards.text: Timeline: When do the cranial and caudal neuropores close during neural tube formation?
cards.answer: Cranial neuropore closes at day 25 (Carnegie stage 11). Caudal neuropore closes at day 28 (Carnegie stage 12). Neural tube fusion begins in the middle (cervical region) and progresses both cranially and caudally during week 4.

tip.tip: Cranial 25, Caudal 28; 'cranial closes first (day 25), caudal catches up (day 28)'

cards.text: List five key derivatives of neural crest cells.
cards.answer: Dorsal root ganglia (sensory), sympathetic ganglia, Schwann cells (myelin in PNS), adrenal medulla, and melanocytes. (Also: branchial arch structures, dentin, part of meninges.)

tip.tip: Remember 'GASSM': Ganglia (dorsal root, sympathetic), Adrenal medulla, Schwann cells, Skin (melanocytes)
